DISRAELI, PEER AND PREMIER, Nitro fiddled while Rome was burning, yet notwithstanding his heartlessness it is said that someone strewed flowers upon his grave. We do not wish to insinuate that Lord Beaconsfield is as cruel as that poten- tate is reputed to have been, but he bids fair to rival him in callousness. When, in the natural order of events, tho present Prime Minister conies to shuffle off his mortal political coil, and in due course receives his apotheosis, we shall certainly not grudge the floral oontributions to hie political tenth, rhetorical and otherwise. In the meantime, however, while Lord Beacons- field is fiddling, or, as the Duke of Argyll put it the other night, " twiddling his thumbs," we must decline to burn incense in his honour. Verily, he is the Prince of triflers, and the habit seems tr be growing upon him with age. We know that people as they arrive a* extreme old age return to second childhood, and recur to the reoulleo- firms and pastimeeof their early year.. lord Beaconsfield really appears to be reverting to the toys and glittering gew- gaws which find their proper place in the domestic nursery and playroom. We pre. some that the Premier is responsible fur the Queen's Speech. Now, we are not disposed to be exacting about the words and phrases which are put into the mouth of ller Majesty by her responsible Ministers, either at the opening or prorogation of Parliament. At the same time, the speech is quite a fitting subject for criticism, with respect to errors either of omission or com- mission. With all Lord Beaconntield's art and dexterity in phrase logy, be has not hitherto been happy either in the matter or the manner of hie Queen's Speeches. Last year the proposed assumption of the title of Empress of India doubtless intended to dazzle and delight the vulgar eye, fell singularly fiat. In many quarters he announcement was received with grumbling and dislike, and in all with indifference. At first Mr. Disraeli declared that the pur- pose of the Queen's assuming the title of Empress was to frustrate the deeigns of Russia upon our Indian frontier. That statement of the Premier was received with incredulity and derision, and was quietly dropped as soon as possible. Indeed, the Royal Titles Bill, like most of Lord Beacons- field's measures, got so mangled, and frittered away in the course of its passing through Parliament, that, to use a Lanca- shire phrase' its own mother must have had difficulty in knowing it. The title became in fact, an appendage only to be used on state occasions, like the obsolete state coach . . .
